item.title: Journify Raises $12M Series A Amid 5x Growth
item.description:
Investors back Journify’s push into the US and Europe

Journify, the ad signal infrastructure company, today announced a $12 million Series A at four times its previous valuation. Al Mada Ventures led the round, co-led by returning investor Silicon Badia, with Shorooq and Bunat Ventures increasing their investment and Du Ventures and Oraseya Capital joining as new investors. The funding will take Journify into the US and Europe and expand the AI behind its platform.

Global ad spend will exceed $1 trillion in 2026, with algorithms expected to place three quarters by 2028, according to dentsu. These systems learn from the customer outcomes brands send back. Browser restrictions, broken tracking, and disconnected offline sales leave them with an incomplete picture of who buys.

Journify makes sure ad platforms such as Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Amazon Ads see the purchases, sign-ups and store sales a brand’s customers actually make. More than 100 businesses use Journify today, from fast-growing ecommerce brands to some of the region’s largest retailers, representing hundreds of millions of dollars in annual ad spend.

Customers include Jarir Bookstore, one of Saudi Arabia’s largest retailers, which increased its return on ad spend on Meta by 182%, and Saudi ecommerce brand Baytonia, which grew its return on ad spend on TikTok by 80% while cutting cost per purchase by 44%.

“AI is transforming advertising, but the intelligence behind it is only as good as the signals it receives,” said Taoufik El Jamali, Co-Founder and CEO of Journify. “Businesses know who buys, who comes back and what creates lasting customer value. Too little of that knowledge reaches the ad platforms driving their growth. Our vision is to close that gap, turning real customer outcomes into intelligence ad platforms can learn from. We’re building toward a future where advertising AI understands what makes a customer valuable to each business, not just what makes them click.”“As AI takes on a greater role in marketing, we believe the connection between reliable customer data and the decisions built on it will become increasingly valuable,” said Omar Laalej, Managing Director at Al Mada Ventures. “What interests us about Journify is its approach to building that connection from the data layer up: a privacy-first foundation that can evolve into intelligence and action. The founders’ understanding of that opportunity gives us confidence in their ability to build a platform that marketers can increasingly rely on, both to understand their customers and to act on that understanding.”Hossam Shafick, Partner at Silicon Badia, Seed Lead and returning investor, added, “Since our initial investment, Journify has grown its valuation by more than 4x, and its revenues more than 5x, validating both the strength of its technology and the team’s ability to execute at scale. That performance has deepened our conviction that Journify can become a global leader in ad signal infrastructure. We are proud to double down and co-lead this round as the company expands into the world’s largest advertising markets.”

Journify already uses AI to monitor every connection continuously, detect signal-quality issues and fix them. The new funding will grow those capabilities as Journify expands beyond the GCC. In the US alone, digital advertising revenue reached $294.6 billion in 2025, according to IAB and PwC.

“I’m excited to help Journify scale in the biggest ad market in the world,” said Ryan Burke, a newly appointed member of Journify’s board and three-time Chief Revenue Officer. “I’ve known Taoufik since our InVision days, and I’ve seen his product execution in action. Based on the success they’re already seeing in the Middle East, it’s not a question whether it works in the US, but how fast we can scale.”

About Journify

Journify builds ad signal infrastructure for performance marketers. Its privacy-first, real-time data layer helps brands improve the quality and reliability of the first-party signals used in advertising and measurement.

Journify connects data across web, mobile, offline sales, CRM, ecommerce platforms, backend systems and data warehouses. It validates and enriches conversion events and activates consented signals server-side across Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap, Amazon Ads and other platforms.

Founded in 2022 by Taoufik El Jamali, Amine Chouki and Omar Al Shoubaki, Journify is headquartered in San Francisco with offices in Dubai and Riyadh. Learn more at journify.io.

Journify has obtained a SOC 2 Type II report and is committed to GDPR compliance.

item.title: Operational risk is business risk: How CIOs safeguard continuity and build resilience
item.description:
Downtime and tampering with operational environments have material, even devastating, impacts on business continuity, the recent cyberattack against refrigeration systems at several large supermarket chains in France being a glaring example of that. The refrigeration system attacks caused significant food waste, a disruption in availability to customers, and the level of financial loss is still being measured. Unfortunately, this costly disruption in operations is not a unique experience: according to Claroty’s 2026 global survey on operational resilience, more than half (51%) of CIOs say they have experienced operational downtime as a result of a cyber incident related to their organization’s cyber-physical systems (CPS).

We’ve experienced additional highly impactful attacks like this in just the past few years, such as the Stryker healthcare supply chain attacks and the Jaguar Land Rover cyberattack. With 27% of CIOs saying downtime has lasted between 3-7 days from their organization’s most significant CPS-related cyber incident, that time could mean millions in financial losses, safety hazards, and interruption of services.

These potentially devastating impacts are the result of the accelerating complexity and scale of threats to operational environments: the convergence of IT and OT, rapid AI adoption, and sprawling third-party exposure. Addressing it requires CIOs to lead a unified, outcome-focused, cross-functional action that tangibly reduces business risk.

Integrate resilience into business continuity and recovery

Gaps in today’s approach to securing operational environments leave organizations ill-equipped to address risk in a way that builds resilience and preserves business continuity. CIOs face a balancing act of proving security outcomes that achieve executive mandates amidst organizational and digital transformation.

While CIOs have been leading their organizations to integrate IT and CPS security governance and risk management—64% reported being mostly or fully integrated—they have yet to take the critical next step of unifying those processes with business continuity under the assumption of an inevitable compromise. Most CIOs (54%) said they were only somewhat confident that their organization’s CPS are adequately accounted for in business continuity and disaster recovery plans.

This highlights the need to modernize business continuity plans for operations. CIOs can establish unified governance across IT and OT by investing in real-time visibility and risk management, and adopting a structured, scenario-driven playbook that includes regular cyber-attack drills and recovery workflows tailored to operational environments. These actions ensure that critical operations can withstand, respond to, and rapidly recover from cyber disruptions, safeguarding business outcomes.

Implement a practical framework for operational resilience

To harness the power of operational resilience, CIOs must start by reorienting programmatic protection toward measurable operational resilience. While overall, those working in CPS-related organizations say that CIOs hold primary accountability for operational protection (39% reported this), budget control and oversight remain fragmented across IT, security, and operations. Establish a unified IT and operational governance model across functions to reduce fragmentation and align operational uptime with enterprise security priorities.

CIOs must also transition business continuity and disaster recovery strategies beyond conventional IT failovers toward comprehensive operational recovery. Mandating routine simulation exercises to evaluate offline system recovery, manual overrides, and segmented safety mechanisms remains crucial for protecting revenue and avoiding physical safety risks.

Resilience requires more than just planning; it also requires a mature, measurable, and cross-functional approach. CIOs are at the helm of modernizing and transforming how their organizations safeguard business continuity through proactive operational resilience programs that withstand and rapidly recover from today’s threats to cyber-physical environments.

Explore Claroty’s latest global research to learn more about how organizations are treating operational resilience as a business imperative to safeguard the world’s most mission-critical infrastructure.

item.title: 7 sure-fire ways to blow your AI budget
item.description:
CIOs have always felt pressure to deploy emerging technologies rapidly. Implementation brings challenges, including calculating and measuring upfront investment costs. Deploy too quickly, and when the hype fades, many IT departments are left with a costly architecture to support, security gaps, and operational issues.

The same trend is happening with AI. Many CIOs procured enterprise-wide AI model licenses and empowered employees to experiment with language models and develop AI agents. Others asked DevOps teams to accelerate AI code generation and vibe coding. The shift from rapid experimentation to deploying more AI capabilities to production can leave CIOs with mounting AI debt and AI FinOps gaps.

CIOs’ near-term concern is managing budgets amid consumption-based AI pricing models. Even as AI token costs decrease, more employees are using AI, and agents are given more challenging, expensive assignments. Here are seven common mistakes IT leaders make that result in blown AI budgets.

Defining an AI strategy without measurable business outcomes

Most CIOs and CAIOs recognize the need to establish AI strategies focused on areas where AI can provide lasting business value. But many fail to quantify targeted business outcomes, leaving employees to use adoption metrics as the primary objective.

“Every token spent on a pilot that never proves its value is money leaders can’t get back and lost opportunity cost, which is a governance failure more than a technology one,” says Rob Scudiere, CTO at Verint. “Every agent and workflow should have to earn its budget by showing results that achieve the desired business outcome, or lose it.”

Kris Beevers, CEO and cofounder of Netbox Labs, says to use existing business metrics to see whether the areas adopting AI are improving them faster. “If adoption is climbing but the outcomes aren’t moving with it, that’s a pretty good signal to rethink where you’re spending,” Beevers says.

Recommendation: Financial impacts may be hard to target during experimental phases, but employees should set financial objectives before moving AI agents into development and deployment phases.

Experimenting without AI governance

CIOs may find they have a real mess on their hands when a few pilot AI agents quickly scale to thousands running in production. Much of AI governance focuses on identifying owners, setting data-access rules, defining target business outcomes, and establishing accuracy guidelines. CIOs must also educate employees on underlying cost factors, including model selection and platform standardization.

“Delayed AI governance gets framed as a compliance risk, but it’s just as much a budgetary concern,” says Guy Bourgault, head of agentic systems at Concentrix. “The longer organizations wait to define ownership, standards, and controls, the more they end up funding inefficiency, rather than progress.”

Varun Goswami, global head of product and AI at Newgen, says AI budgets are wasted on scattered pilots, duplicated integrations, and agents that run quietly without ever proving value. “Build on one governed platform rather than a dozen parallel stacks, reuse templates and connectors instead of custom-building each use case, and match the model to the job rather than routing everything to the priciest foundation model,” Goswami recommends.

Data quality is a third concern, according to Collibra and The Harris Poll, with 96% of IT leaders saying project failure almost always traces back to poor data foundations, and 51% reporting significant staff hours spent manually correcting autonomous AI agent outputs. CIOs should set data quality metrics and establish data products to build a trustworthy AI context layer.

Recommendation: CIOs should update and communicate their AI governance policies monthly, as AI cost, capabilities, compliance, and security considerations evolve rapidly.

Focusing tokenomics on model costs and not business value

Much of the discussion around AI token economics, or tokenomics, focuses on the costs of using different AI models. But the FinOps Foundation defines tokenomics as “the study of how the production, distribution, and consumption of tokens generate business outcomes and AI value within an organization.”

Because many organizations use multiple models, SaaS with AI agents, and internally developed AI agents, CIOs should partner with the CFO to measure total impact, including AI’s direct token costs, employee efforts, ongoing inference costs, and the value delivered.

“Companies can quickly overspend on AI when they focus too narrowly on token consumption, and the starting point should always be the business outcome,” says Prakash Kota, CIO at UKG. “I use the Three T’s: does the work require talent for judgment or expertise, can existing tools solve it efficiently, or do tokens create enough value to justify the investment?”

CIOs should then set AI budgets at the employee, department, and workflow levels. Each group’s budget should be reviewed and adjusted regularly based on outcomes. This discipline promotes fiscally smart decisions about when and how to use AI capabilities and can drive a top-down culture change.

“The same tokens can go to a skilled engineer shipping a product faster, or to a non-expert generating 10 versions of the same slide deck,” says Tom Shea, CEO and cofounder at OneStream. “The line item in the budget looks identical either way, and true token efficacy requires governance to ensure those tokens are empowering experts to accelerate output, rather than fueling a massive cost explosion.”

Recommendation: Setting AI budgets too soon may curtail employees’ enthusiasm in learning and experimenting with AI. Establish financial targets based on a maturity curve to encourage experimentation first, then fiscal discipline when AI agents are deployed to production.

Developing AI agents without standards

CIOs should communicate these two cost considerations to DevOps teams using AI code generators.

First, according to Stack Overflow’s 2026 Developer Survey, 73% of developers use AI coding assistants and agents daily, but developers care more about quality (75%) over cost (38%) when shaping prompts and picking models. CIOs should set guidelines for balancing cost and quality tradeoffs, establish DevOps non-negotiables, and require code analysis in deployment pipelines.

“Coding is no longer a constraint, and the bottleneck has moved to how we ensure the correctness of code,” says Anurag Dhingra, SVP and GM of networking and collaboration at Cisco. “There’s just no humanly possible way to review every piece of code that is written by AI.”

The problem is that 96% of developers don’t fully trust AI-generated code and 48% always check their AI-assisted code before committing, according to Sonar’s State of Code Developer Survey. As large organizations may use several AI code-generating tools, they need to benchmark quality, cost, and developer satisfaction.

“Teams need clear guardrails and engineering standards, especially as AI agents accelerate development and can introduce costly rework,” says Andrea Malagodi, CTO at Sonar. “Having live data aggregated from your one or many providers, to enable you to see the cost per PR [pull request], is a good governance mechanism.”

Recommendation: While AI code generation is a remarkable breakthrough, it also brings new costs and quality considerations CIOs should track.

Using frontier models for all AI needs

Another cost consideration comes as organizations deploy hundreds of AI agents and provide developers several AI models to choose from. Developers may choose models based on preferences rather than performance and cost considerations.

Craig Wiley, VP of AI at Databricks, says 77% of companies now juggle multiple model families because the best model for one task is rarely the best for another. “The flexibility comes at a cost of managing shifting prices, scattered vendors, and zero visibility into where your budget’s actually going. The fix is real-time budgets and smart routing that automatically sends queries to the most cost-effective model,” Wiley says.

Recommendation: Josh Fecteau, chief data and AI officer and CIO at Teradata, says that frontier models are expensive and not necessary for every task. “Diversify your model strategy with cheaper small language models, custom models, and industry-specific models,” Fecteau recommends.

Deploying AI agents without monitoring cost spikes and inefficiencies

A key challenge with AI agents is their variable costs, especially when they are given tasks of varying complexities. While some AI providers are moving to outcome-based pricing models, many still use a license model with a fixed number of tokens, plus consumption-based pricing for overages. This means CIOs must monitor costs, set AI observability standards, and define rules for handling performance variances in AI agents.

“I spent 25 years in telephony where every minute had a price, and agentic AI is the first software I’ve seen that bills like a phone call and gets budgeted like a license,” says CJ Combs, AI strategy executive at Columbus. “AI costs stop being predictable the moment an agent can loop, because it keeps pulling in context, retrying, and calling tools in ways nobody budgeted for.”

Experts suggest several implementation cost inefficiencies to review. Babak Pahlavan, founder, CEO, and CPO at NinjaTech AI, says that AI agent processing duration is an easy indicator. “A single autonomous agent running a multi-hour task can burn a month’s allocation in an afternoon because every tool call, every retry, every piece of context it re-reads gets billed,” Pahlavan says.

Other cost factors require experts to review an AI agent’s decision logs to determine optimization. Adi Elimelech, CTO and cofounder of Jedify, says, “If every query drags an entire database schema back to the LLM, token costs scale with the size of your environment rather than the complexity of the question. The cost compounds, since the model often doesn’t get it right on the first pass and loops back for another round trip before landing on the correct answer.”

Recommendation: CIOs will need to mature several AgenticOps and site reliability engineering practices to monitor AI agents and respond to cost, security, quality, performance, and other incident types.

Building agents without a change management plan

One of the biggest gaps in deploying AI agents is that deployment is just one step in a change management process. AI governance requires identifying agent owners who are accountable for decisions and responsible for outcomes. These owners should also sponsor the underlying change management process.

“The biggest AI cost overruns rarely come from technology,” says Abhijit Kakhandiki, SVP and GM of digital business automation at BMC Software. “They come from organizations deploying AI without redesigning processes, ownership models, and governance.”

Part of the change process requires identifying human-in-the-middle responsibilities to review the agent’s recommendations. The review process builds trust and lets owners switch to autonomous decision-making for low-risk, high-volume, trusted recommendations.

“It’s not going to be a binary switch where, from day one, you’re going to trust AI agents to run tasks autonomously,” says Joel Hellermark, chief AI officer at Workday. “Progressively, they’re going to earn the right to run those workflows autonomously. If it’s your fiftieth time approving an expense below $50 for one of your direct reports that looks exactly on policy, you can trust the agent to run it for you.”

Recommendation: Growing adoption isn’t the end game, but it’s a key step toward delivering business value. Metrics to track adoption include AI response quality, trust scores, repeat usage, and value delivered to adopters.

A simple rule is that you can’t manage what you don’t measure. CIOs should set budgets, track costs, and measure outcomes, especially as more agents move into production.

item.title: Gen Z is driving the death of the legacy helpdesk ticket
item.description:
Much has been made of Generation Z’s supposed inability to adequately conform to modern-day corporate culture.

A recent Business Insider article on Gen Z (born 1997–2012) workplace readiness contains some damning statistics. The piece cites a 2024 poll of nearly 1,000 business leaders, 75% of which described some or all of the recent graduates they hired as “unsatisfactory.” Arguably worse, it cites another 2024 study from Hult Business School, in which 37% of HR leaders said they’d prefer to have a robot or AI do a job than hire a recent new grad, while another 30% said they would rather just leave the job vacant. Quite damning, indeed.

Warranted or not, these complaints about Gen Z are not new.

NYU Stern professor Suzy Welch conducted a September 2025 study juxtaposing the values of incoming Gen Z workers with those of hiring managers. Welch’s study included survey data from 2,100 hiring managers and a behavioral assessment of over 45,000 respondents (7,500 of which were Gen Z).

In a Wall Street Journal Op-Ed, Welch writes, “A mere 2% of Gen Z members hold the values that companies want most in new hires, namely achievement, learning and an unbridled desire to work.” According to Welch’s study, Gen Z members mostly value well-being and self-care, helping others and authenticity and expression. Oh, heaven forbid.

Not to be outdone, in March 2026, another NYU professor wrote a Wall Street Journal Op-Ed on “Why Gen Z is unprepared for the workplace.” The one, from psychology professor Tessa West, laments Gen Z’s lack of communication skills and failure to understand older generations. West writes, “Younger generations—Gen Z specifically—have learned to communicate in a digital world, sending texts and instant messages instead of interacting in person.”

West attributes Gen Z’s poor communication skills to a combination of excessive screen time, online classes during the COVID pandemic and a general overreliance on technologies. I cannot definitively say whether these accusations hold water; however, I do believe that the answer doesn’t lie in replacing humans with AI or leaving roles unfilled. Hiring managers need to adapt to younger generations, whether they want to or not. And we’re seeing this in the help desk software space in real time.

Gen Z has little patience for traditional corporate bureaucracy

Aside from grievances from older folks like me, the fact remains that Gen Z has little patience for traditional corporate bureaucracy. When these younger workers experience a technology glitch, they don’t want to log into a clunky portal, fill out a 10-field form and wait two days for a level 1 support agent to respond. These kids expect instant, consumer-grade, self-service resolution. If the enterprise doesn’t provide it, they’ll just bypass IT entirely.

To overly generalize, most members of Gen Z are comfortable with AI chatbots and tend to search for their own solutions online before reaching out to another human directly. This tendency to rely on mediated communication as opposed to person-to-person communication makes sense given their life experiences with COVID, online coursework, the post-pandemic reevaluation of work culture and their status as a mobile-first generation.

Ramifications for the help desk software space

To retain young talent, enterprises should consider deploying conversational AI, automated self-service password portals and omni-channel support to match the speed at which Gen Z operates.

Self-service should be the first order of operation. Rather than forcing employees to create a ticket and escalate an issue to an agent, workers should have the option to remedy the situation themselves. Across the IT support industry, we’re seeing more emphasis on AI oversight and escalation handling, as opposed to level 1 IT support work.

Additionally, given Gen Z’s mobile-first status, it is vital to have mobile-native applications for internal IT issues. These shouldn’t just be desktop portals reconstructed to fit a mobile interface; these should be mobile apps with consumer-grade quality UX interfaces equipped with things like push notifications for ticket updates.

We’re also seeing more agentic chatbots in the ITSM space. Gen Z workers (and all generations, really) expect agents to be able to handle simpler requests, like access provisioning, password resetting and resolving calendar conflicts.

Omni-channel continuity has become vital too. When Gen Z’ers begin a conversation in Slack or Zoho Cliq, they expect that conversation to seamlessly flow into SMS, email, mobile apps and other corporate channels.

Key takeaway

When it comes to IT service management, Gen Z workers expect agentic self-service, a mobile-first UX, omni-channel support and the ability to resolve tier-1 support issues themselves. Despite the lamentations of some old curmudgeons like me, Gen Z isn’t going anywhere. And what’s more, Gen Alpha (2010 – 2024) is waiting in the wings. If we haven’t brought our service desk infrastructure up to Gen Z’s standards, now is the time.

item.title: Does AI actually save employees time? Data is contradictory
item.description:
It’s early days for AI-assisted work, and sentiments are mixed about its benefits: Does AI actually bring value and save employees time, or does it bog them down and add unnecessary activities?

Data from ActivTrak seems to vacillate between those two potential realities: The latest research from the productivity tracking software company says employees who use AI most heavily are working up to 90 minutes longer each day, yet its previous research, published earlier this year, found that, in general, all employees are actually working less.

The discrepancy may be due in part to the timespan and sample sizes of the data collection for the two reports, but it indicates that enterprises should still be wary of vendor claims about AI-related productivity gains. Measuring them remains incredibly difficult.

AI use compared

ActivTrak’s current findings are based on behavioral work data gathered from 9,140 knowledge workers across 467 enterprises over a five month period (April 1 to September 25, 2026). This sample is much smaller than that of its previous report based on 443 million hours of work performed by 163,638 employees across 1,111 organizations over a three year period (January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2025).

According to the latest findings, heavy AI users are working between 8.42 and 9.08 hours per day, compared to 7.58 hours for those not using AI. ActivTrak’s previous findings revealed that, overall, average workdays had decreased by roughly 9 minutes (a 2% decline).

On the productivity front, heavy AI users have 22% shorter focus sessions than light users (37.8 minutes versus 48.2), suggesting their work is more fragmented due to AI use; further, they switch apps 15% more frequently than non-users.

“Over time, those interruptions add friction to high-value work that requires concentration, critical thinking, and sustained attention,” Sarah Altemus, manager of the ActivTrak Productivity Lab, said in a blog post describing the latest findings.

ActivTrak’s previous report had found that over the period of the earlier study, focus efficiency, the percentage of work time spent in focused, uninterrupted activity, fell to a three year low of 60% with AI use, and average focused session time in 2025 declined by 9% from 2023. However, that same report found that daily productive time increased by 19 minutes, or 5%, to 6 hours and 36 minutes, with AI in the workplace. Furthermore, productive sessions grew by 13%.

The company’s latest report also tracked the productivity differences between users of tools with embedded AI and users of web-based AI tools. Those using embedded AI switched apps 0.6 times an hour, while those using AI on the web switched between 1.7 and 4.2 times per hour. That’s up to 4x more switching than by employees who don’t make use of AI at all, which creates what ActivTrak describes as a “swivel-chair tax” — the additional effort spent by employees due to the movement between apps.

Similarly, in its previous report, ActivTrak had found that, overall, task switching in general rose 12%, or 10-plus minutes during the survey period.

Interestingly, according to the latest research, light users spend more active work time in core job-specific apps (81.4% compared to 78%). “In other words, more frequent AI engagement doesn’t necessarily translate into more focused work,” Altemus pointed out.

The larger issue is the way organizations manage the additional capacity that AI may create, Altemus noted. “When employees complete tasks faster, managers may assume they have room for more responsibilities,” she said. Without clear workload boundaries, time savings may be redirected into additional work that can be taxing.

The numbers often don’t tell the full story

ActivTrak has a useful view of how work moves across applications, noted Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, but he also pointed out that it sells the capability that produces these measurements.

Recorded use depends on what the instrumentation can detect, he observed. For example, an employee can use AI at work and still appear in the non-user group, and work on an unmanaged personal device sits outside the measured estate. In addition, an API or a background agent can finish work without producing a desktop session, and passive screen time, an offline meeting captured through a calendar, and paid hours are also different measures. Furthermore, switching apps is easier to observe than switching attention within an application.

Ultimately, he noted, those judging the value of AI need to establish what happened after the first task became faster. “An improvement per paid hour can conceal effort left off the timesheet,” said Gogia. “The [enterprise] board should be able to say whose day improved and whose work made that improvement possible.”

This article has been updated to clarify that some stats are not related to AI.
